category_defaults._comment: Fallback for a stack with no entry of its own - the common case. Weaker than a real entry, far stronger than stack-agnostic doctrine. The mentor applies these, then researches the framework's own guidance live, and says which is which.

architecture_rules: Transport does transport only. Business rules live in a module that imports no web framework - if the rule can only be reached through a request object, it can only be tested through one.
Testability is the cheapest architecture metric there is. When a rule needs the framework booted to verify, the rule is in the wrong place, not the test.
Persistence sits behind an interface with an in-memory implementation, so the suite runs with no credentials and no container.
Configuration is read in one place and validated at boot. Values read ad hoc across modules fail at the first request instead of the deploy.
Nothing durable lives in process memory. Containers, workers and serverless instances all restart and take it with them.
key_decisions: Persistence: what stores state, and what happens to it between deploys or cold starts.
Authorization model: how an entry point declares who may call it, including 'public on purpose'.
Failure policy at every outbound call: retry with a bound, degrade, fail loudly, or queue.
Configuration and secrets: what is environment, what is code, and how the two are kept apart.
Observability: where an unhandled failure lands where a human will see it.
API contract shape: how a breaking change to a response is versioned or avoided.
operability_rules: Every outbound call states a timeout AND a retry count, including zero. An SDK that retries by default multiplies your timeout - the effective ceiling is the product, not the number you set.
Every entry point states its authorization decision explicitly. An unguarded handler is indistinguishable from a deliberately public one.
No credential in the repository, in a log line, or in anything sent to a client.
An unhandled failure produces a record somewhere a human will see, with enough context to identify the request.
State that must outlive a process restart is not held in process memory. Serverless containers and worker restarts both take it with them.
testing_rules: Untrusted text that reaches an output format - markup, SSML, SQL, a shell, a template - is escaped, and the escaping has its own test. Input from a user or from a model is untrusted.
A write to shared storage does not clobber neighbouring keys, and there is a test that proves it.
Reading a record written by an earlier version does not crash. Data outlives deploys; test the old shape.
Every entry point has a test for its failure response, not only its success response.
Every stated failure policy has a test: the timeout path, the retry exhaustion path, the degraded path. A policy nobody exercised is a hope.

architecture_rules: Presentation is separate from data fetching. A component that fetches and renders cannot be reused or tested without the network.
Business rules live outside components, in plain modules that render nothing.
Shared state has exactly one owner. Two places writing the same state is a bug waiting for a race.
No secret in anything the bundler can reach. Everything in the bundle ships to the browser.
key_decisions: State management: what holds shared state, since almost no framework decides this for you.
Routing and navigation, including deep links and browser history.
Data fetching and caching: what is fresh, what is stale, and who decides.
Styling approach, and where the component library boundary sits.
Form handling and validation: where the rules live and how errors surface.
Build and deploy target, which determines which framework features are even available.

Loading affordance house style: progress bar with percentage for determinate work, skeleton or spinner otherwise. Agree it once with the user and write it into CLAUDE.md rather than deciding per screen.
operability_rules: Every asynchronous operation a user can see declares four states: loading, empty, error and success. Empty is not success with no rows, and success on a mutation is a confirmation, not a silent return to normal.

The loading affordance matches what you actually know: a progress bar with a percentage only when progress is determinate (upload, batch, known steps); a skeleton or spinner when it is not. A percentage you cannot compute is invented, and inventing it teaches the user your indicators mean nothing.
Every interactive element is reachable and operable by keyboard, and focus order follows the visual order.
A state change a user needs to know about is announced, not only displayed - the error message that only renders in colour does not exist for part of your audience.
No secret, key or token reachable from code that ships to the browser.
A user-visible failure says what happened and what to do next. 'Something went wrong' is not a failure policy.
testing_rules: All four async states are covered by tests - loading, empty, error and success. They are presentation rules, and presentation rules are testable.
Presentation rules are testable and are worth testing: that the error shows, that the button disables while submitting, that focus lands where it should.
Untrusted content rendered as markup is escaped, with a test.
Keyboard reachability is a presentation rule like any other. Test it the same way.
Do not assert DOM structure. It changes on every markup refactor and proves nothing about behaviour.

architecture_rules: Apply both the backend and frontend rules; the boundary between them is where the expensive mistakes live.
Anything crossing to the client is a deliberate export. Assume everything reachable from client code is public.
key_decisions: Where the server/client boundary sits, and what crosses it.
How mutations happen, and where their authorization is enforced.
Rendering and caching strategy per route.
Persistence and migrations.
Everything in the backend and frontend lists that the project actually uses.

The loading affordance matches what you actually know: a progress bar with a percentage only when progress is determinate (upload, batch, known steps); a skeleton or spinner when it is not. A percentage you cannot compute is invented, and inventing it teaches the user your indicators mean nothing.
Apply both the backend and frontend rules. The boundary between them is where the expensive mistakes live: a secret crossing to the client, or an action that authorizes on the wrong side.
testing_rules: All four async states are covered by tests - loading, empty, error and success. They are presentation rules, and presentation rules are testable.
Test the boundary explicitly: that a mutation rejects an unauthorized caller, and that no secret is reachable from client code.
Apply both the backend and frontend testing rules.

architecture_rules: Business rules live in plain modules, not in screens. A screen is reached by navigation and cannot be imported cheaply for a test.
Native and platform access goes through a wrapper the tests can replace, or the suite only runs on a device.
Stored data has a versioned shape from the first release. You cannot migrate what you did not version.
key_decisions: Offline behaviour: what happens to an in-flight write when the network drops.
Local storage, and how stored data migrates when the app updates on a device you do not control.
Permissions: what is requested, when, and what the app does when refused.
Crash and error reporting, since you cannot read the user's console.
Deep links and cold-start routing.
Release channel and update strategy - users run old versions for months.

Loading affordance house style: progress bar with percentage for determinate work, skeleton or spinner otherwise. Agree it once with the user and write it into CLAUDE.md rather than deciding per screen.
operability_rules: Every asynchronous operation a user can see declares four states: loading, empty, error and success. Empty is not success with no rows, and success on a mutation is a confirmation, not a silent return to normal.

The loading affordance matches what you actually know: a progress bar with a percentage only when progress is determinate (upload, batch, known steps); a skeleton or spinner when it is not. A percentage you cannot compute is invented, and inventing it teaches the user your indicators mean nothing.
Every feature that writes data states its offline behaviour, even if the decision is 'fail loudly'.
Stored data has a migration path. You cannot ask users to reinstall.
A denied permission is a supported path, not a crash.
Assume several app versions are live at once. A server change that only works with the newest client breaks the rest.
Errors are reported off-device or they are invisible to you.
testing_rules: All four async states are covered by tests - loading, empty, error and success. They are presentation rules, and presentation rules are testable.
The offline path has a test, even when the decision is to fail loudly.
Reading data written by a previous app version has a test. Users skip versions and never reinstall.
The denied-permission path has a test. It is a supported path, not an edge case.
Device end-to-end covers incident-level flows only - it is the slowest and flakiest layer available to you.

architecture_rules: Modules declare their inputs and outputs explicitly. An implicit dependency on ambient state is a change nobody can review.
A change that cannot be applied twice safely cannot be retried, and every automated system retries.
key_decisions: Where state lives and who may change it.
Secret storage and rotation.
Blast radius: what one change can take down.
Rollback procedure, tested rather than intended.
Environment parity: how different staging is from production, and where that difference bites.
operability_rules: Every change states what it can break and how it is reverted.
A rollback nobody has performed is not a rollback plan.
Secrets are referenced, never committed.
A change that cannot be applied twice safely is a change that cannot be retried.
testing_rules: A plan or dry run is the test. Read it before applying; that is the only place the blast radius is visible.
The rollback has been performed at least once. A rollback nobody has run is not a plan.
